disclaimer: This is educational context to help you read trends and ask better questions — not veterinary advice, and not a diagnosis. Lab values must be interpreted by your veterinarian in the context of your cat's history and exam.

interpretation.title: Reading changes over time
interpretation.text: A single result is noisier than it looks. Values move from one sample to the next for reasons that have nothing to do with disease: how the sample was taken and handled (hydration, fasting, stress, time to the lab), the analyzer's own imprecision, and your cat's normal day-to-day biological variation. For a change between two tests to be real, it has to exceed this combined "noise" — the reference change value. SDMA shows this well: a reported 14 can genuinely represent anywhere from about 8 to 20. So trust a trend across several consistent results, not one dip or spike, and the most reliable comparison is against your own cat's healthy baseline rather than the population reference range. Treatment, a recent meal, or IV fluids can also shift values on their own — see each metric's notes below.

dynamics.confounders: Dominated by analytical imprecision — a reported value can swing roughly ±40% (a 14 can represent ~8–20), so small moves are often just noise. Less affected by muscle mass than creatinine; dehydration can nudge it up.
dynamics.monitoring: Use persistent values, not a single reading, and compare against your cat's own baseline. In stable CKD it is typically rechecked every 3–6 months.

Chemistry / IDEXX SDMA.summary: SDMA (symmetric dimethylarginine) is a kidney-filtration marker. It tends to rise earlier than creatinine — when roughly 25–40% of kidney function is lost — so it can flag chronic kidney disease before creatinine does.
Chemistry / IDEXX SDMA.high: A persistent SDMA above the reference interval suggests reduced kidney filtration. IRIS uses it (with creatinine) to stage CKD. A single mildly high value can be a false positive, so it should be rechecked.
Chemistry / IDEXX SDMA.low: Low SDMA is not clinically significant.
Chemistry / IDEXX SDMA.isolation: One high SDMA isn't a diagnosis. It's most meaningful when persistent (repeated, in a hydrated cat) and read together with creatinine, urine specific gravity, and phosphorus.

dynamics.confounders: Rises with dehydration and higher muscle mass; falls with muscle loss. IV fluids can transiently lower it, and a renal diet lowers it modestly.
dynamics.monitoring: Creatinine has high individuality — judge it against your cat's own healthy baseline rather than the reference range. Stable CKD is usually rechecked every 3–6 months, sooner if appetite, thirst, weight, or hydration change.

Chemistry / Creatinine.summary: Creatinine is a waste product cleared by the kidneys; blood levels rise as filtration falls. With SDMA it is the basis of IRIS CKD staging.
Chemistry / Creatinine.high: Elevated creatinine (azotemia) suggests reduced kidney filtration, but can also be pre-renal (dehydration) or, rarely, post-renal (obstruction). Higher muscle mass nudges it up; muscle loss lowers it.
Chemistry / Creatinine.low: Low creatinine is usually unimportant and can reflect low muscle mass.
Chemistry / Creatinine.isolation: Interpret with hydration status and urine specific gravity: a hydrated cat that still can't concentrate urine while azotemic points to kidney disease, whereas dehydration alone can raise creatinine transiently.

dynamics.confounders: Swings with hydration, the most recent meal (high-protein raises it), and GI bleeding; IV fluids and low-protein diets lower it. Less specific than creatinine or SDMA.
dynamics.monitoring: Interpret alongside creatinine and hydration; a fasted sample compares better over time.

Chemistry / BUN.summary: Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) is a protein-breakdown waste product filtered by the kidneys. It is a less specific kidney marker than creatinine or SDMA.
Chemistry / BUN.high: High BUN can reflect reduced kidney filtration, but is frequently raised by dehydration, a recent high-protein meal, or gastrointestinal bleeding.
Chemistry / BUN.low: Low BUN can follow a low-protein diet or liver dysfunction.
Chemistry / BUN.isolation: High BUN with normal creatinine and SDMA is often dehydration, diet, or GI bleeding rather than kidney disease — don't read it alone.

Chemistry / BUN: Creatinine Ratio.summary: The ratio of BUN to creatinine, used to help separate pre-renal causes (e.g. dehydration, GI bleeding) from intrinsic kidney disease.
Chemistry / BUN: Creatinine Ratio.high: A high ratio can suggest dehydration or gastrointestinal bleeding.
Chemistry / BUN: Creatinine Ratio.low: A low ratio can follow a low-protein diet or liver dysfunction.
Chemistry / BUN: Creatinine Ratio.isolation: A derived ratio — only meaningful alongside the BUN and creatinine values it's computed from, plus hydration status.

dynamics.confounders: A recent meal, young age, and a hemolyzed sample raise it; phosphate binders and renal diets lower it.
dynamics.monitoring: Tracked against IRIS stage-specific targets; fasting samples compare best.

Chemistry / Phosphorus.summary: Phosphorus is regulated partly by the kidneys. It is central to CKD monitoring, where IRIS sets stage-specific target ranges.
Chemistry / Phosphorus.high: High phosphorus (hyperphosphatemia) is common as CKD advances and is a target of treatment (diet, binders). Young growing animals run higher.
Chemistry / Phosphorus.low: Low phosphorus has several causes including some endocrine disorders.
Chemistry / Phosphorus.isolation: Most informative in the context of kidney values and calcium — the calcium-phosphorus balance matters more than phosphorus alone.

dynamics.confounders: Total calcium shifts with albumin and can be altered by lipemia; ionized calcium is the more reliable measure.
dynamics.monitoring: Confirm a persistent abnormal with ionized calcium, and read it with phosphorus.

Chemistry / Calcium.summary: Total blood calcium, tightly hormone-regulated. Calcium and phosphorus are interpreted together.
Chemistry / Calcium.high: High calcium has many causes (some hormonal or neoplastic) and warrants follow-up, ideally with ionized calcium.
Chemistry / Calcium.low: Low total calcium is often tied to low albumin and may not reflect true (ionized) calcium.
Chemistry / Calcium.isolation: Total calcium is affected by albumin; an abnormal value is best confirmed with ionized calcium and read alongside phosphorus.

dynamics.confounders: A hemolyzed or delayed sample can read falsely high; IV fluids, diuresis, and poor appetite can lower it.
dynamics.monitoring: Check the hemolysis index before trusting an unexpected change.

Chemistry / Potassium.summary: A key electrolyte for nerve and muscle function, regulated by the kidneys.
Chemistry / Potassium.high: High potassium can occur with urinary obstruction or severe kidney/adrenal disease and can affect the heart. Hemolyzed samples can read falsely high.
Chemistry / Potassium.low: Low potassium (hypokalemia) is common in cats with CKD and can cause weakness.
Chemistry / Potassium.isolation: Check the Hemolysis Index — a hemolyzed sample can spuriously change potassium. Otherwise interpret with kidney values.

Chemistry / Sodium.summary: The major extracellular electrolyte, reflecting water balance more than salt intake.
Chemistry / Sodium.high: High sodium usually reflects water deficit (dehydration).
Chemistry / Sodium.low: Low sodium can reflect fluid shifts or losses.
Chemistry / Sodium.isolation: Read with chloride, hydration status, and the other electrolytes — sodium alone rarely tells the story.

Chemistry / Chloride.summary: An electrolyte that tracks closely with sodium and contributes to acid-base balance.
Chemistry / Chloride.high: High chloride often parallels high sodium (dehydration) or acid-base shifts.
Chemistry / Chloride.low: Low chloride can follow vomiting or acid-base disturbances.
Chemistry / Chloride.isolation: Interpreted alongside sodium and the acid-base picture, not on its own.

dynamics.confounders: Stress at the visit and a recent meal raise it; a delayed or unseparated sample can read falsely low. None of these mean diabetes.
dynamics.monitoring: Fructosamine reflects ~2 weeks and is steadier than a single glucose; at-home or fasted sampling reduces the stress effect.

Chemistry / Glucose.summary: Blood sugar. In cats this is strongly affected by stress at the visit.
Chemistry / Glucose.high: A high glucose in cats is frequently stress hyperglycemia rather than diabetes; fructosamine reflects the prior ~2 weeks and helps tell them apart. Persistent high glucose with clinical signs suggests diabetes.
Chemistry / Glucose.low: Low glucose has several causes and, if real, can be serious; a delayed or mishandled sample can also read falsely low.
Chemistry / Glucose.isolation: One high glucose in a stressed cat usually isn't diabetes — confirm with fructosamine (or repeat at home) before drawing conclusions.

Chemistry / Total Protein.summary: The sum of albumin and globulins in blood; a broad screen interpreted via its two components.
Chemistry / Total Protein.high: High total protein can reflect dehydration or increased globulins (inflammation/immune stimulation).
Chemistry / Total Protein.low: Low total protein can follow loss (gut, kidney, blood) or reduced production.
Chemistry / Total Protein.isolation: Always break down into albumin vs globulin — the components, and their ratio, carry the meaning.

Chemistry / Albumin.summary: The main blood protein made by the liver; helps hold fluid in vessels.
Chemistry / Albumin.low: Low albumin can reflect gastrointestinal loss, kidney loss, liver underproduction, or chronic inflammation. In chronic enteropathy it is usually only mildly low.
Chemistry / Albumin.isolation: Read with globulin and total protein. In suspected gut disease, low albumin is a supportive — not specific — finding.

Chemistry / Globulin.summary: A mixed group of blood proteins including antibodies; reflects immune and inflammatory activity.
Chemistry / Globulin.high: High globulin suggests inflammation, chronic infection, or immune stimulation.
Chemistry / Globulin.low: Low globulin can follow blood or gut loss, or immune deficiency.
Chemistry / Globulin.isolation: Interpreted with albumin (and the A:G ratio); the pattern matters more than the single number.

Chemistry / Albumin: Globulin Ratio.summary: The ratio of albumin to globulin, a pattern marker for inflammation and protein loss.
Chemistry / Albumin: Globulin Ratio.high: A high ratio is rarely a concern on its own.
Chemistry / Albumin: Globulin Ratio.low: A low ratio can reflect low albumin, high globulin, or both — seen with inflammation and some protein-losing conditions.
Chemistry / Albumin: Globulin Ratio.isolation: A derived value — interpret with the albumin and globulin it comes from.

Chemistry / ALT.summary: Alanine aminotransferase, an enzyme that leaks from liver cells when they are injured. A fairly liver-specific marker.
Chemistry / ALT.high: Elevated ALT indicates liver-cell injury, but the magnitude doesn't equal severity and many causes are mild or secondary (including hyperthyroidism in cats).
Chemistry / ALT.low: Low ALT is not clinically significant.
Chemistry / ALT.isolation: A modest ALT rise alone is non-specific. Read with ALP, GGT, bilirubin, and — in older cats — thyroid status.

Chemistry / ALP.summary: Alkaline phosphatase. In cats ALP has a short half-life, so even small elevations can be meaningful.
Chemistry / ALP.high: High ALP in cats can accompany cholestasis (impaired bile flow), hyperthyroidism, or other conditions and warrants follow-up.
Chemistry / ALP.low: Low ALP is not clinically significant.
Chemistry / ALP.isolation: Interpret with the other liver markers and thyroid status rather than alone.

Chemistry / GGT.summary: Gamma-glutamyl transferase, a liver/biliary enzyme that complements ALP for cholestasis.
Chemistry / GGT.high: High GGT supports a cholestatic (bile-flow) pattern of liver disease.
Chemistry / GGT.low: Low GGT is not clinically significant.
Chemistry / GGT.isolation: Best read alongside ALP and bilirubin as part of the cholestasis pattern.

Chemistry / Hemolysis Index.summary: A sample-quality flag indicating red-cell breakdown (hemolysis) in the tube. It is about the specimen, not the patient.
Chemistry / Hemolysis Index.high: A raised hemolysis index means some chemistry results on the same panel may be artifactually altered (e.g. potassium can read falsely high).
Chemistry / Hemolysis Index.low: A normal index means hemolysis is unlikely to be skewing results.
Chemistry / Hemolysis Index.isolation: This value exists precisely to caution interpretation of *other* results — check it before trusting an unexpected abnormal on the same panel.

Chemistry / Lipemia Index.summary: A sample-quality flag indicating fat (lipemia) in the sample, often from a non-fasted draw. It is about the specimen, not the patient.
Chemistry / Lipemia Index.high: A raised lipemia index means some results on the same panel may be artifactually altered.
Chemistry / Lipemia Index.low: A normal index means lipemia is unlikely to be skewing results.
Chemistry / Lipemia Index.isolation: Like the hemolysis index, this is a caution flag for *other* values on the same panel — not a finding in itself.

Chemistry / Cardiopet proBNP (Feline).summary: NT-proBNP is a hormone released when heart muscle is stretched or stressed. The Cardiopet proBNP test screens for heart disease (commonly hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) before symptoms appear.
Chemistry / Cardiopet proBNP (Feline).high: An elevated NT-proBNP raises concern for cardiac disease and typically prompts an echocardiogram to confirm. It is sensitive for severe disease but can miss mild-to-moderate HCM, so a normal result doesn't fully exclude it. Reduced kidney function can also modestly raise it.
Chemistry / Cardiopet proBNP (Feline).low: A low/normal result makes clinically significant heart strain less likely at that moment, but doesn't rule out early disease.
Chemistry / Cardiopet proBNP (Feline).isolation: A blood biomarker, not a diagnosis — abnormal results are confirmed with imaging (echocardiogram), and the value is influenced by kidney function.

dynamics.confounders: Non-thyroidal illness can pull it down into the normal range; methimazole (anti-thyroid medication) lowers it by design.
dynamics.monitoring: After starting or changing methimazole, T4 is rechecked in ~2–3 weeks, then periodically — and watch the kidney values, since treatment can unmask CKD.

Endocrinology / Total T4.summary: Total thyroxine, the main screening test for feline hyperthyroidism — a common disease of older cats.
Endocrinology / Total T4.high: A high Total T4 with compatible signs supports hyperthyroidism. Early or concurrently-ill cats can sit high-normal, sometimes needing additional thyroid tests.
Endocrinology / Total T4.low: Low T4 can occur with non-thyroidal illness; primary hypothyroidism is rare in cats.
Endocrinology / Total T4.isolation: Importantly, hyperthyroidism increases kidney blood flow and can mask underlying CKD — kidney values may look better than they truly are and can worsen once thyroid levels are controlled. Interpret T4 and kidney values together.

dynamics.confounders: Dehydration concentrates it (a falsely reassuring value); IV fluids dilute it. Stress or excitement can transiently raise it in cats.
dynamics.monitoring: Read with hydration status and reticulocytes; CKD-related anemia develops slowly over months.

Hematology / Hematocrit.summary: The fraction of blood made up of red cells; a core measure of anemia or dehydration.
Hematology / Hematocrit.high: A high hematocrit usually reflects dehydration (concentration) rather than true excess red cells.
Hematology / Hematocrit.low: A low hematocrit means anemia. Cats with advanced CKD often develop a mild, slowly-progressive non-regenerative anemia.
Hematology / Hematocrit.isolation: Read with hydration status (a dehydrated anemic cat can look deceptively normal) and the reticulocyte count to judge whether the marrow is responding.

Hematology / RBC.summary: The red blood cell count — the number of red cells, which carry oxygen. It moves together with hematocrit and hemoglobin.
Hematology / RBC.high: A true high count (erythrocytosis) is uncommon; far more often a high value reflects dehydration concentrating the blood, or stress/excitement transiently mobilising red cells in cats.
Hematology / RBC.low: A low count means anemia. Whether the marrow is responding is judged by the reticulocyte count (regenerative vs non-regenerative).
Hematology / RBC.isolation: Interpret alongside hematocrit, hemoglobin, hydration status, and reticulocytes rather than on its own.

Hematology / Hemoglobin.summary: The concentration of hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein in red cells. It tracks closely with the red cell count and hematocrit.
Hematology / Hemoglobin.high: Usually reflects dehydration (concentration) or stress rather than a true excess of red cells.
Hematology / Hemoglobin.low: A low hemoglobin indicates anemia. Read with the reticulocyte count to see whether the marrow is regenerating.
Hematology / Hemoglobin.isolation: Lipemia or hemolysis in the sample can falsely raise the measured value, so read it together with the red cell count and hematocrit.

Hematology / MCV.summary: Mean cell volume — the average size of the red cells. It classifies anemia as small-celled (microcytic), normal (normocytic), or large-celled (macrocytic).
Hematology / MCV.high: Larger cells (macrocytosis) often accompany a regenerative response (young red cells are larger); in cats it can also occur with certain marrow disorders or FeLV.
Hematology / MCV.low: Smaller cells (microcytosis) classically suggest iron deficiency (e.g. chronic blood loss) or portosystemic liver shunting.
Hematology / MCV.isolation: Most useful read with MCHC and the reticulocyte count; a small average-size shift is not meaningful in isolation.

Hematology / MCH.summary: Mean cell hemoglobin — the average amount of hemoglobin per red cell. It moves in parallel with MCV and MCHC.
Hematology / MCH.high: A high value is usually an artifact of lipemia or hemolysis in the sample rather than a true finding.
Hematology / MCH.low: A low value reflects red cells with less hemoglobin, as in iron deficiency.
Hematology / MCH.isolation: A calculated index best read alongside MCV, MCHC, and the red cell count, not on its own.

Hematology / MCHC.summary: Mean cell hemoglobin concentration — how concentrated the hemoglobin is within the red cells (normochromic vs hypochromic).
Hematology / MCHC.high: A true high is not biologically possible; an elevated MCHC almost always means hemolysis or lipemia in the sample interfered with the measurement.
Hematology / MCHC.low: A low MCHC (hypochromia) accompanies regeneration (young cells are less hemoglobinised) and iron deficiency.
Hematology / MCHC.isolation: Interpret with MCV and the reticulocyte count; treat a high value as a likely sample artifact first.

Hematology / RDW.summary: Red cell distribution width — how variable the red cells are in size (anisocytosis). It often rises before the average size (MCV) shifts.
Hematology / RDW.high: A wider distribution means more variation in cell size, which can accompany a regenerative response or early iron deficiency.
Hematology / RDW.low: A low RDW is not clinically significant.
Hematology / RDW.isolation: A sensitive but non-specific flag; read with MCV and the reticulocyte count to understand what kind of cells are driving the variation.

Hematology / Reticulocytes.summary: The absolute count of reticulocytes — newly released, immature red cells. In cats the laboratory aggregate reticulocyte count is the key measure of whether the marrow is regenerating.
Hematology / Reticulocytes.high: A raised reticulocyte count means the marrow is regenerating, as expected when anemia is caused by blood loss or red cell destruction (hemolysis).
Hematology / Reticulocytes.low: A low or normal count in the face of anemia means the response is non-regenerative — the marrow isn't keeping up — as seen with chronic kidney disease, inflammation, or marrow disease.
Hematology / Reticulocytes.isolation: Only meaningful alongside the degree of anemia; the same count can be normal or inadequate depending on how anemic the cat is.

Hematology / % Reticulocyte.summary: The percentage of red cells that are reticulocytes (young red cells). The absolute reticulocyte count is the more reliable measure of regeneration.
Hematology / % Reticulocyte.high: A higher percentage suggests the marrow is producing new red cells, but a percentage can look high simply because the total red cell count is low.
Hematology / % Reticulocyte.low: A low percentage with anemia points to a non-regenerative process.
Hematology / % Reticulocyte.isolation: Prefer the absolute reticulocyte count, and read it against how anemic the cat actually is.

Hematology / % Reticulocytes.summary: The percentage of red cells that are reticulocytes (young red cells). The absolute reticulocyte count is the more reliable measure of regeneration.
Hematology / % Reticulocytes.high: A higher percentage suggests the marrow is producing new red cells, but a percentage can look high simply because the total red cell count is low.
Hematology / % Reticulocytes.low: A low percentage with anemia points to a non-regenerative process.
Hematology / % Reticulocytes.isolation: Prefer the absolute reticulocyte count, and read it against how anemic the cat actually is.

Hematology / Reticulocyte Hemoglobin.summary: The hemoglobin content of the youngest red cells (reticulocytes) — a near-real-time readout of whether enough iron is reaching the marrow to build new red cells.
Hematology / Reticulocyte Hemoglobin.high: A high value is not typically a concern.
Hematology / Reticulocyte Hemoglobin.low: A low value flags iron-restricted red cell production (e.g. iron deficiency from chronic blood loss) earlier than the standard indices do.
Hematology / Reticulocyte Hemoglobin.isolation: A forward-looking marker best read with MCV, MCHC, and the reticulocyte count when iron deficiency is being considered.

Hematology / WBC.summary: The total white blood cell count — the body's circulating immune cells. Changes are interpreted from the differential (which cell types changed), not the total alone.
Hematology / WBC.high: A high count (leukocytosis) commonly reflects inflammation, infection, or — very often in cats — a stress or excitement (adrenaline) response.
Hematology / WBC.low: A low count (leukopenia) can reflect overwhelming infection consuming cells, or reduced marrow production; in cats it raises concern for viral disease.
Hematology / WBC.isolation: Always read the differential: the same total can mean very different things depending on which white cell type is driving it.

Hematology / Neutrophils.summary: The absolute neutrophil count — the front-line cells against bacterial infection and inflammation. This absolute number is more meaningful than the percentage.
Hematology / Neutrophils.high: Neutrophilia accompanies inflammation and infection, and also a stress (steroid) response, which is common in cats.
Hematology / Neutrophils.low: Neutropenia can reflect consumption in severe infection or reduced marrow production, and warrants attention.
Hematology / Neutrophils.isolation: Read with the rest of the differential and the clinical picture; a stress pattern and an inflammatory pattern can look similar on the count alone.

Hematology / % Neutrophils.summary: The percentage of white cells that are neutrophils. The absolute neutrophil count (also reported) is the number to judge.
Hematology / % Neutrophils.high: A higher share of neutrophils can reflect inflammation, infection, or a stress response — but a percentage shift can also just mirror a change in another cell line.
Hematology / % Neutrophils.low: Interpret a low percentage via the absolute neutrophil count.
Hematology / % Neutrophils.isolation: Percentages always sum to 100%, so one going up forces others down; rely on the absolute counts.

Hematology / Lymphocytes.summary: The absolute lymphocyte count — immune cells central to antibody and viral defense. Judge this absolute number rather than the percentage.
Hematology / Lymphocytes.high: Lymphocytosis in cats is frequently a transient adrenaline (excitement) response; it can less commonly reflect chronic immune stimulation or lymphoid disease.
Hematology / Lymphocytes.low: Lymphopenia is most often a stress (steroid) effect, and can also occur with acute viral infection or loss of lymph fluid.
Hematology / Lymphocytes.isolation: Read with the full differential and the cat's stress level at sampling.

Hematology / % Lymphocytes.summary: The percentage of white cells that are lymphocytes. The absolute lymphocyte count is the more meaningful figure.
Hematology / % Lymphocytes.high: A higher share can reflect excitement or immune stimulation, but may simply mirror a fall in another cell type.
Hematology / % Lymphocytes.low: Interpret via the absolute lymphocyte count.
Hematology / % Lymphocytes.isolation: Because percentages are interdependent, rely on the absolute counts.

Hematology / Monocytes.summary: The absolute monocyte count — cells that clean up tissue debris and support chronic inflammation.
Hematology / Monocytes.high: Monocytosis can accompany inflammation, tissue damage, or a stress response.
Hematology / Monocytes.low: A low monocyte count is not clinically significant.
Hematology / Monocytes.isolation: A supporting clue read alongside the neutrophil count and clinical picture, not a standalone finding.

Hematology / % Monocytes.summary: The percentage of white cells that are monocytes. The absolute count is the number to judge.
Hematology / % Monocytes.high: A higher share may reflect chronic inflammation, or simply mirror changes in other cell lines.
Hematology / % Monocytes.low: Interpret via the absolute monocyte count.
Hematology / % Monocytes.isolation: Rely on the absolute counts rather than the percentage.

Hematology / Eosinophils.summary: The absolute eosinophil count — cells involved in allergic and parasitic responses.
Hematology / Eosinophils.high: Eosinophilia classically points to parasites (e.g. fleas, intestinal worms) or allergic/hypersensitivity conditions; some feline syndromes raise it markedly.
Hematology / Eosinophils.low: A low eosinophil count is usually a stress (steroid) effect and is not a concern on its own.
Hematology / Eosinophils.isolation: Most informative with history (parasite exposure, skin or airway signs) rather than in isolation.

Hematology / % Eosinophils.summary: The percentage of white cells that are eosinophils. The absolute count is the more meaningful figure.
Hematology / % Eosinophils.high: A higher share suggests an allergic or parasitic process; confirm with the absolute count.
Hematology / % Eosinophils.low: Interpret via the absolute eosinophil count.
Hematology / % Eosinophils.isolation: Rely on the absolute counts rather than the percentage.

Hematology / Basophils.summary: The absolute basophil count — a rare white cell type involved in allergic and parasitic immunity. Normally present in very low numbers in cats.
Hematology / Basophils.high: Basophilia is uncommon and, when present, tends to accompany the same allergic or parasitic conditions that raise eosinophils.
Hematology / Basophils.low: A low or zero basophil count is normal and not significant.
Hematology / Basophils.isolation: A minor finding interpreted alongside the eosinophil count.

Hematology / % Basophils.summary: The percentage of white cells that are basophils — normally very low.
Hematology / % Basophils.high: A higher share is uncommon; confirm with the absolute count and read with the eosinophils.
Hematology / % Basophils.isolation: Rely on the absolute counts rather than the percentage.

dynamics.confounders: Feline platelets clump extremely readily, which falsely lowers the automated count — so a low number is very often an artifact, not true thrombocytopenia. A blood-smear estimate is used to confirm.
dynamics.monitoring: A genuinely low count is rechecked (often on a fresh, well-mixed sample) and confirmed on a smear before it is acted on.

Hematology / Platelets.summary: The platelet count — the cell fragments that form clots. In cats this is the count most prone to laboratory artifact.
Hematology / Platelets.high: A high count (thrombocytosis) in cats is usually a reactive response to inflammation or other stimuli rather than a primary problem.
Hematology / Platelets.low: A truly low count (thrombocytopenia) can raise bleeding risk, but in cats a low automated value is far more often caused by platelet clumping than by real disease.
Hematology / Platelets.isolation: Don't act on a low automated platelet count without a smear estimate to rule out clumping; true thrombocytopenia is uncommon in cats.

dynamics.confounders: Drops after IV fluids, diuretics, or a big drink of water; a fresh, pre-fluid sample is the most informative.
dynamics.monitoring: Most meaningful paired with blood kidney values from the same visit.

Urinalysis / Specific Gravity.summary: Urine specific gravity (USG) measures how concentrated the urine is — a direct readout of the kidneys' concentrating ability.
Urinalysis / Specific Gravity.high: Well-concentrated urine (cats typically concentrate above ~1.035) suggests the kidneys are conserving water effectively.
Urinalysis / Specific Gravity.low: Dilute urine, especially alongside elevated kidney values, is a hallmark of reduced concentrating ability in CKD. It can also follow other causes of increased drinking.
Urinalysis / Specific Gravity.isolation: USG is the key partner to blood kidney values: azotemia *with* dilute urine points to kidney disease, whereas azotemia with concentrated urine suggests dehydration. Always read them together.

Urinalysis / Glucose.summary: Glucose (sugar) in the urine. Healthy cats have none; it appears only when blood glucose climbs high enough to spill past the kidneys (~250–300 mg/dL).
Urinalysis / Glucose.high: Glucose in the urine (glucosuria) most often reflects persistently high blood sugar — a key supporting finding for diabetes. Brief stress hyperglycemia can occasionally cause transient glucosuria as well.
Urinalysis / Glucose.isolation: Confirm with blood glucose and ideally fructosamine — a single positive, especially in a stressed cat, is not a diabetes diagnosis on its own.

dynamics.confounders: Blood or infection in the sample, and normal day-to-day variation, move it; the dipstick is only a screen.
dynamics.monitoring: Quantify and trend with a UPC ratio on a clean sample — UPC itself has notable biological variation, so rely on several measurements.

Urinalysis / Urine Protein.summary: A dipstick estimate of protein in urine. Proteinuria is a risk factor for CKD progression; IRIS substages CKD by the urine protein:creatinine (UPC) ratio.
Urinalysis / Urine Protein.high: Protein in urine can indicate kidney involvement, but the dipstick is only a screen — it must be confirmed and quantified with a UPC ratio on a sample without blood or infection.
Urinalysis / Urine Protein.low: Absence of dipstick protein is reassuring but doesn't fully exclude low-level proteinuria.
Urinalysis / Urine Protein.isolation: A positive dipstick alone isn't meaningful — it needs a UPC ratio and an inactive sediment (no blood/infection) to interpret for CKD substaging.

Chemistry / AST.summary: Aspartate aminotransferase is a "leakage" enzyme found in both liver and muscle cells; it rises when those cells are injured.
Chemistry / AST.high: A high AST means liver-cell or muscle damage. It is less liver-specific than ALT, so AST up alongside ALT points to the liver, while AST up with a high creatine kinase points to muscle.
Chemistry / AST.low: Low AST is not clinically significant.
Chemistry / AST.isolation: Read with ALT (liver) and creatine kinase (muscle) to localize the source; a rough blood draw can nudge it up on its own.

Chemistry / Bilirubin - Total.summary: Bilirubin is a pigment from the breakdown of red cells that the liver processes and excretes in bile; total bilirubin is the sum of its conjugated and unconjugated forms.
Chemistry / Bilirubin - Total.high: A high total bilirubin causes jaundice and points to one of three things: increased red-cell destruction (pre-hepatic), liver disease, or obstructed bile flow (post-hepatic). In cats even mild elevations matter, and hepatic lipidosis is a common cause.
Chemistry / Bilirubin - Total.low: Low bilirubin is not clinically significant.
Chemistry / Bilirubin - Total.isolation: Interpret with the conjugated/unconjugated split, the liver enzymes, and red-cell values (hematocrit, reticulocytes) to find the cause.

Chemistry / Bilirubin - Conjugated.summary: The water-soluble form of bilirubin already processed by the liver. It accumulates mainly when bile flow is impaired (cholestasis).
Chemistry / Bilirubin - Conjugated.high: A higher conjugated fraction points toward liver disease or bile-duct obstruction.
Chemistry / Bilirubin - Conjugated.isolation: Read with total bilirubin and the cholestatic enzymes (ALP, GGT).

Chemistry / Bilirubin - Unconjugated.summary: The form of bilirubin produced from hemoglobin breakdown before the liver conjugates it.
Chemistry / Bilirubin - Unconjugated.high: A higher unconjugated fraction suggests red-cell destruction (hemolysis) outpacing the liver's processing.
Chemistry / Bilirubin - Unconjugated.isolation: Read with total bilirubin and red-cell values (hematocrit, reticulocytes).

Chemistry / Cholesterol.summary: A blood lipid carried in the bloodstream; values are affected by recent meals and by several hormonal and metabolic conditions.
Chemistry / Cholesterol.high: High cholesterol is often simply post-meal, but can accompany diabetes, cholestatic liver disease, or kidney disease with protein loss.
Chemistry / Cholesterol.low: Low cholesterol can reflect liver insufficiency (including portosystemic shunts) or protein-losing conditions.
Chemistry / Cholesterol.isolation: Most meaningful on a fasted sample and read with the rest of the panel.

Chemistry / Creatine Kinase.summary: Creatine kinase (CK) is a leakage enzyme concentrated in muscle — the most specific marker of muscle-cell damage. It rises and clears quickly.
Chemistry / Creatine Kinase.high: A high CK means muscle injury, which ranges from trivial (a rough blood draw, an injection, or a cat that has been recumbent/anorexic) to significant trauma or muscle disease.
Chemistry / Creatine Kinase.low: Low CK is not clinically significant.
Chemistry / Creatine Kinase.isolation: A mild rise is often handling-related; interpret with AST and the clinical picture rather than alone.

Chemistry / Amylase.summary: An enzyme historically associated with the pancreas. In cats it is not a reliable test for pancreatitis.
Chemistry / Amylase.high: In cats a high amylase is non-specific — it is not diagnostic for pancreatic disease and can rise simply with reduced kidney clearance.
Chemistry / Amylase.low: Low amylase is not clinically significant.
Chemistry / Amylase.isolation: Feline pancreatitis is assessed with pancreas-specific tests (e.g. fPL / SpecfPL) and imaging, not amylase.

Chemistry / Lipase.summary: An enzyme released by the pancreas. Standard ("catalytic") lipase is a poor test for pancreatitis in cats.
Chemistry / Lipase.high: A high catalytic lipase is non-specific in cats and is also affected by kidney function and other organs.
Chemistry / Lipase.low: Low lipase is not clinically significant.
Chemistry / Lipase.isolation: Don't read catalytic lipase alone for feline pancreatitis — pancreas- specific lipase (fPL / DGGR) and imaging are used instead.

Chemistry / TCO2 (Bicarbonate).summary: Total CO2 is essentially a measure of blood bicarbonate, the body's main acid buffer, and is part of acid-base balance.
Chemistry / TCO2 (Bicarbonate).high: A high value (metabolic alkalosis) can follow vomiting of stomach acid or certain electrolyte disturbances.
Chemistry / TCO2 (Bicarbonate).low: A low value (metabolic acidosis) accompanies conditions that add acid or lose bicarbonate — kidney disease, diabetic ketoacidosis, or poor perfusion.
Chemistry / TCO2 (Bicarbonate).isolation: Interpret with the anion gap, electrolytes, and the cat's clinical status.

Chemistry / Anion Gap.summary: A calculated estimate of "unmeasured" acids in the blood, derived from the electrolytes; a screen for metabolic acidosis.
Chemistry / Anion Gap.high: A widened anion gap suggests a build-up of acids such as ketones (diabetic ketoacidosis), lactate (poor perfusion), or certain toxins, or kidney failure.
Chemistry / Anion Gap.low: A low anion gap is uncommon and usually just reflects low albumin.
Chemistry / Anion Gap.isolation: A calculation read with TCO2/bicarbonate and the electrolytes, not alone.

Chemistry / Na: K Ratio.summary: The ratio of sodium to potassium — a quick screening flag derived from two electrolytes.
Chemistry / Na: K Ratio.high: A high ratio is generally not a concern.
Chemistry / Na: K Ratio.low: A low Na:K ratio (from high potassium and/or low sodium) classically prompts consideration of Addison's disease (rare in cats), but is more often due to kidney/urinary disease, GI losses, body-cavity effusions, or sample handling.
Chemistry / Na: K Ratio.isolation: Interpret the actual sodium and potassium values and the clinical picture, not the ratio on its own.

Chemistry / Osmolality.summary: The concentration of dissolved particles in blood — driven mostly by sodium, glucose, and urea — reflecting the body's water balance.
Chemistry / Osmolality.high: High osmolality indicates a relative water deficit (dehydration) or high glucose or urea.
Chemistry / Osmolality.low: Low osmolality indicates a relative water excess.
Chemistry / Osmolality.isolation: Interpret with sodium, glucose, urea, and hydration status.

Chemistry / IDEXX Cystatin B (Urine).summary: Cystatin B is a urine marker of active kidney tubular injury — it is released when tubule cells are damaged, so it reflects ongoing injury rather than overall filtration (unlike creatinine and SDMA).
Chemistry / IDEXX Cystatin B (Urine).high: A value at or above the lab's cutoff suggests active or recent kidney tubular injury and warrants a closer look.
Chemistry / IDEXX Cystatin B (Urine).low: A low value suggests a lower likelihood of active injury.
Chemistry / IDEXX Cystatin B (Urine).isolation: A newer marker interpreted alongside creatinine, SDMA, urine specific gravity, and the clinical picture.

Endocrinology / Free T4 (ng/dL).summary: The unbound, active fraction of thyroid hormone. It is a confirmatory test for hyperthyroidism used to clarify a borderline total T4 — not a first-line screen, because it can read falsely high in cats that are sick for other reasons.
Endocrinology / Free T4 (ng/dL).high: A high free T4 supports hyperthyroidism, but only when read alongside a high or high-normal total T4.
Endocrinology / Free T4 (ng/dL).low: A low free T4 can occur with non-thyroidal illness.
Endocrinology / Free T4 (ng/dL).isolation: A high free T4 with a low total T4 usually reflects other illness rather than thyroid disease; interpret with total T4 and clinical signs.

Endocrinology / Free T4 (pmol/L).summary: The unbound, active fraction of thyroid hormone (reported in SI units). A confirmatory test for hyperthyroidism used to clarify a borderline total T4, not a first-line screen.
Endocrinology / Free T4 (pmol/L).high: A high free T4 supports hyperthyroidism, but only when read alongside a high or high-normal total T4.
Endocrinology / Free T4 (pmol/L).low: A low free T4 can occur with non-thyroidal illness.
Endocrinology / Free T4 (pmol/L).isolation: A high free T4 with a low total T4 usually reflects other illness; interpret with total T4 and clinical signs.

Urinalysis / pH.summary: How acidic or alkaline the urine is, influenced by diet, time since eating, and acid-base status.
Urinalysis / pH.high: Alkaline urine (higher pH) can follow a meal or certain diets, or a urinary infection with urease-producing bacteria, and favours struvite crystals.
Urinalysis / pH.low: Acidic urine (lower pH) is common in cats on meat-based diets and favours calcium oxalate crystals.
Urinalysis / pH.isolation: Read on a fresh sample (pH drifts as urine sits) and together with the sediment (crystals, bacteria).

Urinalysis / Ketones.summary: Ketones are byproducts of fat metabolism, normally absent from urine.
Urinalysis / Ketones.high: Ketones in the urine most often accompany diabetic ketoacidosis, but can also appear with prolonged anorexia or fasting.
Urinalysis / Ketones.isolation: Read with blood glucose — ketones plus high glucose is a diabetic-emergency flag.

Urinalysis / Blood / Hemoglobin.summary: The dipstick "blood" pad detects heme, which can come from intact red cells, free hemoglobin, or muscle myoglobin — it can't tell them apart.
Urinalysis / Blood / Hemoglobin.high: A positive can mean true bleeding into the urinary tract (stones, inflammation, infection, tumour) or hemoglobin/myoglobin in the blood.
Urinalysis / Blood / Hemoglobin.isolation: Always confirm against the sediment — a positive pad with no red cells on microscopy points to hemoglobin or myoglobin rather than bleeding.

Urinalysis / Bilirubin.summary: Bilirubin (a bile pigment) detected on the dipstick.
Urinalysis / Bilirubin.high: Any bilirubin in cat urine is abnormal and can be an early sign of liver disease or red-cell breakdown (unlike dogs, cats should not have bilirubin in their urine).
Urinalysis / Bilirubin.isolation: Read with blood bilirubin and the liver enzymes.

Urinalysis / Urobilinogen.summary: A pigment derived from bilirubin in the gut. The urine dipstick pad is of limited diagnostic value in animals.
Urinalysis / Urobilinogen.high: Results are unreliable and are not used to diagnose disease on their own.
Urinalysis / Urobilinogen.isolation: Generally not interpreted in isolation; liver assessment relies on blood tests.

Urinalysis / Color.summary: The urine's colour, normally pale to dark yellow depending on how concentrated it is. Red or brown can indicate blood, hemoglobin, or myoglobin; very dark can indicate bilirubin; colourless suggests very dilute urine.
Urinalysis / Color.isolation: Interpret with the specific gravity and the sediment/chemistry pads rather than on its own.

Urinalysis / Clarity.summary: How clear or cloudy the urine is. Cloudiness (turbidity) can come from cells, crystals, mucus, or debris.
Urinalysis / Clarity.isolation: Cloudiness is a prompt to examine the sediment; clear urine can still contain abnormalities.

Urinalysis / Collection Method.summary: How the sample was obtained — cystocentesis (a needle into the bladder), free catch, or catheter — which affects how the results are read.
Urinalysis / Collection Method.isolation: Cystocentesis is cleanest for assessing infection (bacteria or blood in a free-catch sample may be contamination) but can add a little blood; note the method when reading the sediment.

Urinalysis / Red Blood Cells.summary: Red blood cells seen in the urine sediment under the microscope.
Urinalysis / Red Blood Cells.high: Increased red cells (hematuria) can come from inflammation, infection, stones, trauma (including the collection needle), or tumours anywhere along the urinary tract.
Urinalysis / Red Blood Cells.low: None to a few is normal — a few are common right after cystocentesis.
Urinalysis / Red Blood Cells.isolation: Read with the collection method and the rest of the sediment.

Urinalysis / White Blood Cells.summary: White blood cells seen in the urine sediment.
Urinalysis / White Blood Cells.high: Increased white cells (pyuria) suggests inflammation or infection of the urinary tract.
Urinalysis / White Blood Cells.low: None to a few is normal.
Urinalysis / White Blood Cells.isolation: Read with bacteria in the sediment and the collection method; pyuria plus bacteria supports infection.

Urinalysis / Bacteria.summary: Bacteria seen in the urine sediment.
Urinalysis / Bacteria.high: True bacteriuria suggests a urinary tract infection, especially with white cells present — but free-catch samples are often contaminated.
Urinalysis / Bacteria.isolation: Interpret with white cells and the collection method; a culture (ideally from cystocentesis) is the gold standard for confirming infection.

Urinalysis / Epithelial Cells.summary: Cells shed from the lining of the urinary and genital tract into the sediment.
Urinalysis / Epithelial Cells.high: Small numbers are normal; many cells can reflect inflammation or, rarely, abnormal cells worth a closer look.
Urinalysis / Epithelial Cells.isolation: Usually a minor finding read with the rest of the sediment.

Urinalysis / Casts.summary: Cylindrical "molds" formed inside the kidney tubules and flushed into the urine.
Urinalysis / Casts.high: A few hyaline casts can be normal, but increased or cellular/granular casts point to active kidney tubular injury.
Urinalysis / Casts.isolation: A specific clue to kidney (tubular) injury, read with the blood kidney values and urine specific gravity.

Urinalysis / Crystals.summary: Mineral crystals that can form in urine; the type (e.g. struvite, calcium oxalate) matters more than their mere presence.
Urinalysis / Crystals.high: Crystals can be normal — especially in urine that has sat or cooled — but some types relate to stone risk or specific conditions.
Urinalysis / Crystals.isolation: Interpret with urine pH, how fresh the sample is, and any history of stones; crystals alone don't equal disease.

Urinalysis / Mucus.summary: Mucus threads in the urine sediment.
Urinalysis / Mucus.high: Small amounts are usually unimportant; more can reflect contamination or lower-tract irritation.

Serology / FeLV Antigen (ELISA).summary: A screening test for feline leukemia virus (FeLV) that detects viral antigen in the blood.
Serology / FeLV Antigen (ELISA).high: A positive (antigen-detected) result indicates FeLV infection and should be confirmed by a second method — a single positive in a healthy, low-risk cat can be a false positive.
Serology / FeLV Antigen (ELISA).low: A negative is reassuring, but a recently exposed cat may need retesting.
Serology / FeLV Antigen (ELISA).isolation: Confirm positives and interpret with the cat's risk and clinical status, per AAFP guidance.

Serology / FIV Antibody (ELISA).summary: A screening test for feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV) that detects antibodies to the virus.
Serology / FIV Antibody (ELISA).high: A positive (antibody-detected) result suggests FIV exposure or infection; because vaccinated cats and kittens with maternal antibody can also test positive, positives are confirmed and read with the history.
Serology / FIV Antibody (ELISA).low: A negative is reassuring; retest if recent exposure is possible, since antibodies take weeks to appear.
Serology / FIV Antibody (ELISA).isolation: Confirm and interpret positives per AAFP guidance, accounting for vaccination and age.

Serology / Heartworm Antigen.summary: A test that detects antigen from adult heartworms.
Serology / Heartworm Antigen.low: In cats a negative does NOT rule it out — cats often have very few worms or single-sex/immature infections, so antigen tests miss many cases.
Serology / Heartworm Antigen.isolation: In cats, interpret a negative cautiously and pair it with antibody testing and imaging, per American Heartworm Society guidance.

Parasitology / Ova & Parasites - Zinc Su.summary: A fecal flotation (zinc-sulfate centrifugation) that concentrates and detects parasite eggs and cysts under the microscope.
Parasitology / Ova & Parasites - Zinc Su.high: Finding ova or parasites confirms infection.
Parasitology / Ova & Parasites - Zinc Su.low: "None seen" lowers the likelihood but doesn't eliminate it — shedding is intermittent and some parasites are missed.
Parasitology / Ova & Parasites - Zinc Su.isolation: A negative flotation with ongoing signs may warrant repeat testing or antigen tests, per CAPC.

Parasitology / Roundworm Antigen.summary: An antigen test for roundworms (Toxocara) that detects the worms directly, catching infections the microscope misses (single-sex worms, or worms not yet shedding eggs).
Parasitology / Roundworm Antigen.isolation: Complements fecal flotation; CAPC recommends routine fecal screening.

Parasitology / Hookworm Antigen.summary: An antigen test for hookworms that detects the worms directly, catching infections the microscope can miss.

Parasitology / Whipworm Antigen.high: A positive indicates whipworm antigen; note that true feline whipworm infection is rare in North America, so positives are interpreted carefully.
Parasitology / Whipworm Antigen.low: A negative is the expected, reassuring result.

Parasitology / Flea Tapeworm Antigen.summary: An antigen test for the flea tapeworm (Dipylidium caninum).
Parasitology / Flea Tapeworm Antigen.high: A positive indicates tapeworm antigen and goes hand-in-hand with flea control.
Parasitology / Flea Tapeworm Antigen.isolation: Interpret with the cat's flea exposure and history.

Parasitology / Cystoisospora Antigen.summary: An antigen test for Cystoisospora, a single-celled (coccidian) intestinal parasite.
Parasitology / Cystoisospora Antigen.high: A positive indicates infection — most significant in kittens or cats with diarrhea.
Parasitology / Cystoisospora Antigen.isolation: Interpret with the cat's age and any GI signs.

relationships.reason: Both estimate kidney filtration (GFR); SDMA usually rises earlier. IRIS stages CKD on the two together.
Both are nitrogenous wastes cleared by the kidneys; BUN is the less specific of the two.
The ratio is computed from BUN and creatinine to separate pre-renal causes from kidney disease.
The ratio is computed from BUN and creatinine to separate pre-renal causes from kidney disease.
Azotemia with dilute urine points to kidney disease; azotemia with concentrated urine suggests dehydration.
Reduced filtration is far more convincing when the kidneys also can't concentrate urine.
Phosphorus rises as CKD advances and is managed by IRIS stage.
Calcium and phosphorus are hormonally co-regulated; the balance is read together.
Hypokalemia is common in cats with CKD.
Advanced CKD often causes a mild non-regenerative anemia (low hematocrit).
Proteinuria substages CKD (via UPC) and predicts progression.
Total protein is the sum of albumin and globulins; interpret by its components.
Total protein is the sum of albumin and globulins; interpret by its components.
The albumin-vs-globulin pattern distinguishes loss, inflammation, and dehydration.
The ratio is derived from albumin and globulin.
The ratio is derived from albumin and globulin.
Chloride normally tracks sodium; divergence flags acid-base shifts.
Read as an electrolyte panel reflecting hydration and renal/adrenal function.
A hemolyzed sample can make potassium read falsely high — check the index first.
Hepatocellular injury (ALT) vs cholestasis (ALP) — the pattern guides interpretation.
ALP and GGT together describe a cholestatic (bile-flow) pattern.
Hyperthyroidism raises kidney blood flow and can mask CKD; treating it may unmask azotemia.
Hyperthyroidism increases GFR and can keep kidney markers deceptively low.
Hyperthyroidism commonly causes mild elevations in liver enzymes.
Hyperthyroidism commonly causes mild elevations in liver enzymes.
Reduced kidney clearance can modestly raise NT-proBNP, so interpret cardiac biomarker with renal function.

conditions.name: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)
conditions.summary: A common, progressive loss of kidney function in older cats. Diagnosis and monitoring center on filtration markers (creatinine, SDMA), the kidneys' ability to concentrate urine, proteinuria, phosphorus, potassium, blood pressure, and anemia.
missing_markers: Urine protein:creatinine ratio (UPC) — needed for IRIS proteinuria substaging
Systolic blood pressure — needed for IRIS hypertension substaging

staging.note: IRIS stages CKD on persistent fasting creatinine and/or SDMA in a hydrated, stable cat, then substages by proteinuria (UPC) and blood pressure. The bands below orient a single value; they are not a stage.

conditions.name: Hyperthyroidism
conditions.summary: Overactive thyroid, common in older cats. Screened with Total T4. It speeds metabolism, can mildly raise liver enzymes, and — importantly — increases kidney blood flow, which can mask underlying CKD until the thyroid is treated.

metrics.role: May be masked low; watch after treatment
May be masked low; watch after treatment

missing_markers: Free T4 by equilibrium dialysis / T3 — for ambiguous high-normal T4 cases

conditions.name: Heart Disease (HCM screening)
conditions.summary: Feline heart disease — most often hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — is often silent on routine bloodwork. The NT-proBNP (Cardiopet) biomarker screens for cardiac strain; abnormal results are confirmed with an echocardiogram.
missing_markers: Echocardiogram — the confirmatory test; bloodwork alone cannot diagnose HCM
Blood pressure — hypertension contributes to cardiac changes

conditions.name: IBD / Small Cell Lymphoma
conditions.summary: Chronic inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and low-grade (small cell) intestinal lymphoma sit on an overlapping spectrum and cannot be told apart by blood tests alone — distinguishing them requires intestinal biopsy with special testing. Bloodwork plays only a supporting role.

metrics.role: May be mildly low with chronic GI loss/inflammation

missing_markers: Cobalamin (vitamin B12) and folate — key GI markers, not on these panels
Intestinal biopsy with histopathology / clonality (PARR) — required to distinguish IBD from lymphoma

conditions.name: Systemic Hypertension
conditions.summary: Persistently high blood pressure, common in senior cats and usually secondary to another disease — most often chronic kidney disease or hyperthyroidism. It is diagnosed by measuring blood pressure, not by bloodwork, but its common causes show up on these panels. Left untreated it damages the eyes, kidneys, heart, and brain.

metrics.role: CKD is a leading cause and consequence

missing_markers: Systolic blood pressure measurement — the actual diagnostic (>160 mmHg generally warrants treatment; <140 is ideal)
Fundic (retinal) exam — to check for hypertensive damage to the eyes
signs: Sudden blindness, a cloudy or bloody eye, or persistently dilated pupils
Often none — hypertension is frequently silent until organ damage occurs

conditions.name: Diabetes Mellitus
conditions.summary: Inadequate insulin action causing persistently high blood sugar. In cats a single high glucose is usually just stress; diabetes requires persistent hyperglycemia with sugar spilling into the urine and clinical signs, often confirmed with fructosamine.

metrics.role: Persistent hyperglycemia — not one stressed reading
Glucosuria — sugar appears in urine above ~250-300 mg/dL

missing_markers: Fructosamine — reflects ~2 weeks of glucose and separates true diabetes from stress hyperglycemia
signs: Weight loss despite a normal or increased appetite
Walking on the hocks (plantigrade stance) in advanced cases

conditions.name: Neoplasia (Cancer)
conditions.summary: Cancer risk rises with age. Most cancers cannot be screened for with routine bloodwork — they are found by physical exam, imaging, and sampling tissue (cytology or biopsy). Bloodwork is occasionally abnormal, but normal results do NOT rule cancer out.

metrics.role: Occasionally high with some cancers (paraneoplastic) — not a screen
May be low (anemia) with some cancers — non-specific

missing_markers: Physical exam, imaging (radiographs / ultrasound), and cytology or biopsy — how cancer is actually found and confirmed
signs: New or growing lumps, or sores that don't heal
Unexplained weight loss, or persistent appetite/energy changes
Vomiting, diarrhea, difficulty breathing, or bleeding

conditions.name: Osteoarthritis
conditions.summary: Degenerative joint disease affects most older cats but is easily missed — cats rarely limp obviously; they slow down instead. There is no blood test for it: diagnosis is by physical exam and joint radiographs.
missing_markers: Orthopedic exam and joint radiographs — the basis of diagnosis; no bloodwork marker exists
signs: Reluctance to jump up or down, or not jumping as high as before
Stiffness, hesitation on stairs, sleeping more
Reduced grooming (a matted or greasy coat), overgrown nails, irritability when handled

conditions.name: Cognitive Dysfunction
conditions.summary: An age-related decline in brain function (feline dementia). There is no blood test; it is a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out medical causes such as hyperthyroidism, hypertension, or pain. Its signs are summarized by the acronym DISHA-AL.
missing_markers: Behavioral assessment plus a medical work-up to exclude other causes — there is no bloodwork marker
signs: Disorientation; changed interactions with people or other pets
Altered sleep cycles; house-soiling; more (often night-time) vocalization
Changes in activity, anxiety, or learning and memory (the 'DISHA-AL' signs)

conditions.name: Dental Disease
conditions.summary: Periodontal disease and painful tooth and gum conditions are very common in older cats and largely hidden. Bloodwork doesn't detect it; a full assessment needs an oral exam and dental radiographs under anesthesia.
missing_markers: Oral examination and dental radiographs under anesthesia — required to assess the teeth and gums
signs: Bad breath, drooling, or blood-tinged saliva
Dropping food, chewing on one side, or pawing at the mouth
Reduced appetite or reluctance to eat dry food

life_stages.name: Kitten
life_stages.summary: Rapid growth and development. Care centers on vaccination, parasite control, infectious-disease testing, and spay/neuter rather than the chronic diseases of older cats.

watch.text: Retrovirus testing (FeLV/FIV), intestinal parasites, vaccination series, congenital problems.

life_stages.screening: Kitten visit series with deworming and core vaccinations; establish a healthy baseline.

life_stages.name: Young Adult
life_stages.summary: Generally the healthiest stretch of life. The goal is prevention and establishing baseline lab values to compare against later.

watch.text: Weight gain / obesity, dental disease, retrovirus status; behavioral and environmental needs.

life_stages.screening: Annual wellness exam; baseline bloodwork and urinalysis so future changes have a reference point.

life_stages.name: Mature Adult
life_stages.summary: The age when age-related disease starts to appear, often silently. Routine screening becomes valuable: even apparently healthy cats in this group are sometimes found to have early kidney disease or hyperthyroidism.

watch.note: Watch for the earliest changes — SDMA plus urinalysis can flag CKD before creatinine rises.
Onset becomes more common; Total T4 screens for it.
Periodontal disease is common and hidden; needs an oral exam.
Weight and appetite changes warrant glucose +/- fructosamine.

watch.text: Also watch for weight gain / obesity and early neoplasia.

life_stages.screening: Begin routine screening around age 7: at least annual exam with bloodwork (including SDMA and Total T4), urinalysis, and blood pressure.

life_stages.name: Senior
life_stages.summary: The highest-risk stage. In one 2-year study, ~54% of senior cats that were apparently healthy at the start developed a clinically relevant disease — most often chronic kidney disease, hyperthyroidism, chronic GI/liver/ pancreas disease, or cancer. Many of these are silent early and best caught by screening.

watch.note: Most common senior disease; combine bloodwork with urinalysis to catch it early.
Common in seniors; Total T4 screens for it, and it can mask kidney disease.
Cardiac disease risk rises; NT-proBNP can screen, confirmed by echocardiogram.
Chronic enteropathy and low-grade intestinal lymphoma become more common.
Often secondary to CKD or hyperthyroidism; needs a blood pressure check.
Persistent hyperglycemia with glucosuria and weight loss.
Cancer risk rises; mostly found by exam/imaging, not bloodwork.
Affects most older cats; they slow down rather than limp.
Common, painful, and hidden; needs an oral exam.
Feline dementia — a diagnosis of exclusion.

life_stages.screening: Twice-yearly exams with at least annual bloodwork, urinalysis, blood pressure, and Total T4. Re-test promptly if appetite, weight, thirst, or activity change.
